passages.title: Understanding English Tenses
passages.content:
English tenses are verb forms that indicate when an action occurs - in the past, present, or future. The present perfect tense, for example, connects the past with the present. It is formed using 'have/has' + past participle and is used to describe experiences, changes, or actions that have relevance to the present moment.

The present perfect continuous tense shows that something started in the past and is continuing at the present time. It is formed using 'have/has been' + present participle (-ing form). This tense is particularly useful when we want to emphasize the duration of an action.

Conditional sentences express hypothetical situations and their consequences. The third conditional, using 'had + past participle' in the if-clause and 'would have + past participle' in the main clause, expresses regret about past situations that cannot be changed.

passages.title: Articles in English
passages.content:
Articles are words that define a noun as specific or unspecific. English has two types of articles: definite (the) and indefinite (a, an). The definite article 'the' is used when we are talking about a specific item that both the speaker and listener know about.

The indefinite articles 'a' and 'an' are used when we are talking about something for the first time or something that is not specific. 'A' is used before consonant sounds, while 'an' is used before vowel sounds. It's important to note that it's the sound, not the letter, that determines which article to use.

There are also cases where no article is needed, called the zero article. This occurs with plural countable nouns when talking in general, with uncountable nouns when talking in general, and with proper nouns.
